newsitem.title: USA: No tobacco settlement without papers - Fla. says.
newsitem.headline: No tobacco settlement without papers - Fla. says.

text.p: Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth said on Monday there could be no broad settlement with the tobacco industry until cigarette makers release all documents pertaining to their manufacturing.
"There will be no settlement until these documents are given to the Congress so that it is in a position to take action," Butterworth said in an interview during a break in a court hearing.

Butterworth, who was among the attorneys general who negotiated a tentative settlement with the tobacco companies last month, challenged them to "stop all appeals regarding the release of cigarette documents and let all the documents go public."

He referred to the tobacco companies' request that Florida's 4th District Court of Appeal reverse a decision allowing secret documents from the Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett Group to be used in Florida's lawsuit against the tobacco industry.
Jury selection is scheduled to start on Friday in the state's lawsuit seeking to recover the public cost of tobacco-related illness.

Last week the appeals court upheld a ruling by Judge Harold Cohen of Palm Beach County Circuit Court that the documents were not protected by attorney-client privilege because they involved alleged illegal attempts by the tobacco industry to deceive the public about the dangers of smoking.
Cohen was scheduled to hear arguments Monday on several pretrial motions in the Florida lawsuit.
An attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., Stephen Kriegbaum, said the documents ruling could have a broad impact on the right to consult lawyers in private.
"The attorney-client privilege is the longest recognized in law and it applies to all Americans," Kriegbaum said.

The tobacco companies have asked that the suit be dismissed on grounds that they have complied with a 1969 federal law governing advertising and product labeling, and that the federal law supersedes the state law that allowed the lawsuit.
The state has argued that the tobacco companies acted in concert to mislead the public about the dangers of smoking, and therefore state fraud laws apply.
